answers.reasoning: Block 10 describes the judge's five-step perturbation check (change input, call recalc_workbook, re-read output), and block 19 notes an agent that never recalculates cannot check its own dynamic values; the page frames this as alignment, not proven causation.
answers.answer: The judge checks perturbation by changing an input, recalculating, and seeing whether the output moves to the right new value. An agent that never recalculates never sees whether its own outputs update, so hardcoded intermediates, overwritten formulas or non-converging circular structures go unnoticed and later fail the judge's check. The link is plausible correlation, not proven cause.

answers.reasoning: The toy widget and failure-mode section show hardcodes pass Output Validation but fail Perturbation; the other options would push values off reference and be caught by a value check.
Block 14 says modifying an existing workbook imposes brittle integration constraints from existing formulas, layouts and references; block 21's case studies show linking errors driving scores.
answers.answer: Synthesis is flexible: the agent designs its own layout. Manipulation forces it to fit into existing formulas, layouts and references, which imposes brittle integration constraints. For example, in the OpEx schedule task, off-by-one row references to the Inputs tab dropped Gemini to 32%, and in the merger model nobody exceeded 35% because of bad links to existing tabs.
